PET PHOTO → PRINTABLE PATTERN

How to turn a pet photo into a cross stitch pattern

Start with a clear cat or dog photo, crop close to your pet, convert it into a grid of thread colors, then check the eyes and markings before exporting a PDF. The goal is a recognizable pet and a project you are willing to stitch.

Pet2Stitch makes a digital chart you stitch by hand. It does not supply a finished portrait or a materials kit. The current prototype PDF download is free.

Try your pet’s photo →

1. Choose a photo where the face is easy to see

Pick a sharp photo with visible eyes, nose and distinctive markings. Compare a few photos before starting: a tiny face in a wide scene gives the grid less room for your pet’s features. Watch for bright white fur blending into a light background or a dark muzzle disappearing into shadow.

2. Crop around the part you want to stitch

Upload your photo, open Crop & edit background, and crop around the head or upper body. Leave room for the ears. For a portrait, removing empty surroundings lets more of your chosen grid describe the face.

Use the erase brush for areas you want to leave as bare fabric. The plain-background shortcut works by color similarity, so check pale fur, whiskers and ears afterwards. Restore any pet detail it removes. White thread and blank fabric are different: erased cells are left unstitched, while white fur can still use white floss.

3. Compare size before committing to a big project

The size slider controls the longest side, not both dimensions. A 120 × 120 pattern has 14,400 grid squares; a 160 × 160 pattern has 25,600. Some squares may be blank. Increasing the size can preserve more detail, but also increases the work.

Square examples on 14-count Aida
GridFinished stitched areaGrid squares before blanks
80 × 805.7 × 5.7 inches6,400
120 × 1208.6 × 8.6 inches14,400
160 × 16011.4 × 11.4 inches25,600

Finished width in inches = stitch width ÷ fabric count. These sizes exclude the extra fabric you need around the design for finishing. Your actual photo crop may produce a rectangular chart.

4. Check colors and isolated stitches

Compare a few thread-color limits in the preview. Fewer colors can reduce thread changes but may merge eye, nose or fur details. More colors can retain shading but add scattered stitches. Look at the symbol chart as well as the simulated stitched view.

Check both eyes, the outline of the nose, and the markings that make the pet recognizable. The optional stray-stitch simplification only changes some subtle isolated cells; it cannot judge whether a portrait looks right. Thread references are approximate screen matches. Compare them with physical floss before buying materials.

5. Download and inspect the PDF

The PDF includes a cover, symbol charts and a thread key with stitch counts. Open it before printing and check that you can distinguish the symbols. Blank cells remain unstitched. You need to buy Aida fabric, floss, a needle and a hoop separately.

Can a complete beginner stitch a pet portrait?

You can use the converter without previous stitching experience, but making a photographic portrait is a larger commitment than generating its chart. Try a small practice design first to learn full cross stitches, counting and changing thread. Then choose a close crop and review how many stitches your pet pattern contains. Pet2Stitch has not yet been validated through beginner trial stitching, and it does not estimate completion time.

Can I use it for a pet memorial?

Yes. You can make a chart from a photo you want to keep close, or create a gift for someone who loves their pet. Review the preview carefully before starting: an automated conversion may need cropping or background edits to preserve the expression you remember.
